title: Visit levels far above national patterns in the hospital and nursing facilities
what_we_see: Subsequent hospital visits were billed at the top level (99233) 73.7% of the time, against 37.2% nationally. Every initial hospital visit was the top level (99223), against 59.5%. Subsequent nursing facility visits were the second-highest level (99309) 95.6% of the time, against 48.8%, and every initial nursing facility visit was the top level (99306), against 48.5%. Both discharge-day families were billed only at the longer code. All 31 assisted living visits were billed with a new-patient code (99344), 25 of them by the nurse practitioner, and none with an established-patient code, although 103 assisted living residents were billed care management in October. In CMS data the physician's top-level share of hospital follow-up visits was 64.5% in 2023, 1.3% in 2024 and is 73.7% now. As billed, the physician's visits alone carry 1.25 to 1.7 times the work units of the median family physician. In October there were 218 visits to 135 nursing facility residents, 1.6 each. Fourteen residents were seen four or more times. Each visit needs a medical reason in the note. Visits with no documented reason for their frequency were the most common failure in the Inspector General's 2026 audit, which sampled residents seen three or more times in a month.
rule: The level of a visit must follow the complexity of medical decision making, or total time, that the note documents for that day, and the service must be medically necessary. A sick population can justify a high average. It does not justify the same level on nearly every visit.
exposure: The difference between adjacent levels is roughly $20 to $45 a visit. On about 6,000 visits a year, a finding that half were one level high would be on the order of $60,000 to $100,000 a year, and Medicare contractors extrapolate from samples. Nationally, 25.5% of the dollars paid for the top initial nursing facility code, which this practice bills on every admission, were improper in Medicare's 2025 review. In Medicare's 2025 review, 22.7% of payments for the top subsequent hospital code (99233), the practice's most-billed visit code, were improper. The Florida Medicare contractor lists hospital visits (99221 to 99223 and 99231 to 99233) as an active targeted review. In July 2026 the Inspector General reported on 60 sampled patient-months of nursing home visits, each with 3 to 10 visits, paid by another contractor in 2018 and 2019. Forty-two failed review: 24 because the visits were not medically necessary, 13 for coding and 10 for missing or insufficient records. A nationwide audit of these services opened in April 2026.
recommended_review: Through the attorney, hire an independent certified auditor to review 10 notes per code family for each clinician, about 80 to 100 notes, chosen at random from the last six months. Ask for under-coding as well as over-coding. Include 10 assisted living visits and check each patient's history for an earlier visit by the practice. Agree with the attorney beforehand what error rate will trigger a larger, statistically valid sample. The Inspector General's self-disclosure protocol asks for at least 100 claims.
control: Quarterly audit of 10 charts per clinician. A monthly table of each clinician's level mix against the national mix. Coding education built from the audit's findings. Levels chosen by the clinician in the note, never changed downstream.

title: Nursing facility claims went out as skilled stays; a visit-pattern rule now sets the long-term code
what_we_see: Until November 10, 2026 every nursing facility visit and every care-management line in the five nursing buildings carried place of service 31, the code for a patient in a Medicare Part A covered skilled stay. Place of service 32, for residents who are not in such a stay, was never used. The payments confirm it: in 2026 Medicare paid $63.28 for the first hour of complex care management in those buildings, which is the skilled-stay rate. On November 10, 2026 the owner set a rule and the billing back end now applies it when a charge is entered: care management in a nursing building is billed as 32, the monthly visit as 32, and weekly or twice-weekly visits, admissions and anything unclear as 31. The rule reads the visit pattern on the chart. It does not read each facility's list of residents in a Part A stay. It reached the live billing branch at 11:14 UTC that day as rule version 2026-11-10.4, and version 2026-11-10.6, live at 22:46 UTC, added the reviewers' follow-ups. The first live batch (12:39 UTC: 60 visits, 66 lines, $10,368, none failed) entered 24 Brynwood visits at 32 and 6 at 31, the one Aspire visit at 31, 28 hospital visits at 21 and 1 assisted living visit at 13. Both initial nursing facility visits went in at 31. Whether AdvancedMD kept every 32 has not been read yet.
rule: Medicare's manual says to use place of service 31 when the patient is in a Part A skilled stay and 32 when the patient is not, even in the same building. The setting changes the payment: 31 pays the facility rate and 32 the non-facility rate. Since July 2025 Medicare compares every line billed as 32 with the facility's Part A claim. A line that does not match is returned with reason code 58, or is paid and later repriced. A 2016 Medicare question-and-answer sheet said care management cannot be billed for a resident in a Part A covered stay. The current sheet does not repeat that limit, and which code fits a month with some Part A days is unsettled.
exposure: Two kinds. Money left unclaimed in the past: from November 2025 through October 2026 Medicare paid 1,667 care-management lines in the nursing buildings, $85,176 in all, none at the long-term rate. At the long-term rate the same lines would have been allowed $76,549 more, of which Medicare's share is $60,015. The owner decided on November 10, 2026 not to ask Medicare to reopen paid claims. From now on the risk runs the other way: a line billed as 32 for a resident who was in a Part A stay that month is an error in the practice's favor. A 2023 Inspector General audit found $22.5 million paid nationally on 1.13 million lines coded 32 during Part A stays. The rule keeps unclear cases at 31, and a line Medicare returns or reprices is reported to the owner and is not changed or resent without his word.
recommended_review: Ask each facility for its monthly list of residents in a Part A skilled stay, with start and end dates. Compare one month of claims billed as 32 with that list. Read the next feed reports: each has a place-of-service line with counts and chart numbers, and says whether AdvancedMD stored the code that was sent. The first batch's import register had not reached the live branch by 14:32 UTC on November 10, so the first read of a stored 32 comes from a later batch.
control: The rule in the feed import, with its own self-test and a line in every feed report. A monthly Part A list from each facility as the proof. Any line Medicare returns with reason code 58 or reprices goes to the owner the same week.

title: 149 October visits were entered under the other clinician by the charge import
what_we_see: Since October 28, 2026 the practice enters its own charges from the Claimocity feed. Until November 10 the import kept one clinician per patient per batch: the last message it read. When a resident's care-management charge (the physician's) and the nurse practitioner's visit charges arrived in the same batch, the visits were entered under the physician. Comparing each feed message's own clinician with the clinician entered shows 149 visits and 167 charge lines, all with October 2026 dates of service and all but one visit in the October 28 batch. On 165 lines (148 visits) the feed names the nurse practitioner and the charge was entered under the physician. On 2 care-management lines (1 visit) it is the other way round. Fees on the 167 lines total $24,438. On November 10, 133 of the lines were billed and not yet paid (120 of them at Medicare), 15 were not yet billed and 19 were paid ($1,711, none of it by Medicare). Only 3 lines are with a Medicaid plan, so this is not the set of Medicaid visits moved to the physician in September. The owner replied the same day that not every nursing visit is the nurse practitioner's. Whether the clinician on a Claimocity charge is always the person who saw the patient is his to confirm. The same check found 18 visits whose code does not fit the building they were entered in: 3 with nursing facility codes entered at the hospital, 2 with hospital codes entered at an assisted living building, 2 care-management visits entered at the hospital and 11 with nursing facility codes entered with no building. The registers do not keep each message's own building, so the building side cannot be sized exactly. None of these has been corrected in AdvancedMD.
rule: A claim must name the clinician who performed the service. Medicare pays a nurse practitioner's service at 85% of the physician fee schedule amount. A payment received under the wrong clinician includes the difference, and an overpayment must be returned within 60 days of being identified.
exposure: If the 120 Medicare lines are paid under the physician, about 15% of each payment is more than Medicare owes on every visit that was the nurse practitioner's: at most about $1,400 on roughly $9,100 of payments (Medicare pays the physician $78.07 and the nurse practitioner $66.36 for the usual follow-up visit). The larger cost is the pattern: 136 visits already billed under a clinician the feed does not name is the kind of finding an auditor extends to other months. No earlier month is affected. Before October 28 charges came in by another route, and every batch that held no care-management charge for the patient entered each visit under the clinician its message names.
recommended_review: Decided by the owner on November 10, 2026 for the 15 lines not yet billed, which are 12 of the 84 feed visits that were never billed (see that finding): the 10 visits that are not initial visits are moved to the nurse practitioner before they are sent, and the 2 initial visits stay under the physician (the owner, 15:18 UTC: 'i saw those patients'). Still open, with no word from the owner to correct them: the 133 lines billed and not yet paid and the 19 paid lines. For those the choices are a corrected claim, or for a paid line a corrected claim or a refund of the difference. The list of visits (chart, visit, date, codes) is rebuilt at any time by tools/feed/feed_clinician_audit.py.
control: Since rule version 2026-11-10.4 reached the live billing branch at 11:14 UTC on November 10, 2026 the import takes the clinician, the building and the admission date from each visit's own feed message. The import counts any visit it could not match to its own message, and the feed report names those visits. Once a month, run the audit tool: it compares every entered visit with the feed.

title: Initial nursing facility visits now go in under the physician; 982 past ones stand under the nurse practitioner's code
what_we_see: The owner's rule, in his words on November 10, 2026: 'going forward the 99306 should always be billed under [the physician's] npi and group npi as i am the one who is doing the initial hps 99306 and 99497'. Rule version 2026-11-10.6, live on the billing branch since 22:46 UTC that day, applies it from the next feed import: every initial nursing facility visit (99306), with the advance care planning line (99497) billed with it, goes in under the physician and the group, whatever clinician the feed message names. Past claims are not reopened or corrected, and are not listed as work; the owner wrote 'it looks like the initial 99306 billing under arnpo has been fixed mostly for 2026'. The billing history holds 982 initial nursing facility visits under the nurse practitioner's code (946 of 99306 and 36 of 99305): 48 in 2022 (from July), 143 in 2023, 522 in 2024, 224 in 2025 and 45 in 2026. The pattern starts in July 2023. From April 2024 to May 2025, 610 of 663 initial visits (92%) were under her code. From June 2025 to November 9, 2026, 422 were under the physician's code and 99 under hers. On the 982 visits $249,340 was charged and insurance payments of $88,061 are posted, $29,641 of it from Medicare Part B. Since October 28, 2026 the feed has named the nurse practitioner on 10 initial visits and the physician on 9.
rule: A claim must name the clinician who performed the service. Medicare allows a nurse practitioner's visit at 85% of the physician amount, and the billing history shows Medicare, Capital Health Plan, Humana and WellCare allowing her initial visits at exactly that share. In a Medicare Part A skilled stay the physician must personally perform the federally required initial comprehensive visit, no later than 30 days after admission; a nurse practitioner may bill a medically necessary first evaluation. A billing record shows only the code a visit was entered under. Only the visit note, who wrote and signed it, shows who saw the patient.
exposure: Going forward, every initial visit goes out under the physician's number. That is right only when he personally did the visit. If the nurse practitioner does one, it must be billed under her. Since October 28 the feed has named her on 10 of the 19 initial visits, so what is logged in Claimocity and what is billed can now differ. The past visits stand as billed: the owner did not ask for past claims to be corrected.
recommended_review: Fix it at the source: the person who logs an initial visit in Claimocity logs it under the clinician who saw the patient, so the feed and the claim agree. If the nurse practitioner does an initial visit, tell billing so that visit goes out under her. A workbook of the 982 past visits was given to the owner on November 10, 2026. No work on past claims is planned: the owner did not ask for any.
control: The import enters every 99306 and its 99497 under the physician (rule version 2026-11-10.6), and the feed report names each initial visit it entered under the physician when the feed named another clinician. The monthly clinician check does not list these visits: it only counts the initial visits entered under the physician by the owner's rule. The feed report's line is where each one shows, so read it. For each skilled admission, record the date of the physician's own comprehensive visit.

title: 84 feed visits could never bill although their chart has a plan
what_we_see: Proven on November 10, 2026 by two independent read-only reviews. 84 feed visits (102 charge lines, $18,802, 39 charts, service dates October 12 to November 7, 2026) were entered while the chart had no insurance plan, so AdvancedMD kept an empty insurance-order list on each. When a plan reached the chart later, the insurance check skipped the save because the visit's order already read '1', and it logged success. A visit with an empty list builds no claim and appears in no Claims Center column: none of the 84 was ever in the Unbilled column across 458 scans, and none of 5,228 billed visits has an empty list. 69 of the 84 ($15,616) were released after the look-up added the chart's first plan; 15 ($3,186) were held and their plan came later. The check's HOLD is only a label in its report: AdvancedMD does not read it, and 56 held visits on charts with a plan were billed anyway. None of the 84 has been billed yet.
rule: A claim is paid only if it is filed within the payer's limit: for Medicare one year from the date of service, and as little as six months for Florida Medicaid plans. A visit that never becomes a claim earns nothing. AdvancedMD lists such a visit on no work list, so only a read of the visit's own insurance order finds it.
exposure: $18,802 of charges, none billed yet. The oldest service date is October 12, 2026, so no filing limit has passed. Whether each payer the look-up found is right is not yet tested, so the $18,802 is not a forecast of collections. The fix went live on November 11, 2026. It has not yet been seen working on a live batch, and the 84 visits are still to be sent.
recommended_review: The owner answered on November 10, 2026 at 15:15 UTC: 'yes to all your recommendations'. So: the 71 visits whose payer only the look-up found go out only after an eligibility check dated to each service date shows the plan active; the one chart with two plans goes to the plan that check shows active; the 13 visits whose plan came from the feed, a face sheet or by hand are sent; the nurse practitioner's visits entered under the physician are moved to her first (10 visits), and the two initial visits stay under the physician (15:18 UTC: 'i saw those patients'). A standing word lets a routine save such a visit again once its first plan lands, after read-backs of the clinician, the admission date and the insurance order, and never on a billed visit. The fix has been live since November 11, 2026. A billing session with write access to the billing system sends them, one pilot visit first; none has been sent yet.
control: The fix, rule version 2026-11-10.7, checks the insurance-order list after every save, never saves a billed visit when it repairs a never-billed one, reads the admission date before and after, words a hold by what the list shows, and adds a daily read-only list of feed visits that were never billed. It passed three independent reviews, a fix round and a re-check, and went live on the billing branch at 01:20 UTC on November 11, 2026. The ten billing self-tests that were run before delivery passed on the delivered version. An eleventh, which was not run before delivery, failed on it: its own stand-in for the billing system was out of date, and no fault was found in the fix. That test was repaired, extended from 51 to 100 checks and checked independently, and all eleven pass on the live branch since 03:05 UTC on November 11, 2026. The same check named three weak spots in the visit-save helper that are older than the fix and not known to have caused harm; a guard for the first of them (never send a save when the visit's charges could not all be read) is being built and reviewed before the 84 visits are sent. The fix has not yet been seen working on a live batch.

title: No coding audit and no compliance program on record
what_we_see: The practice has written billing rules and runs the monthly exclusion check. Nothing else of a compliance program is evidenced: no named compliance contact, no training record, no audit, no log of problems found and fixed. Billing is run by software agents under standing rules that include automatic write-offs.
rule: A compliance program is voluntary for a small practice, but federal guidance describes seven elements and treats a working program as evidence of good faith. The duty to return overpayments is not voluntary. Since 2025 it is triggered when a practice knows of an overpayment, deliberately avoids learning of one, or recklessly disregards the signs.
exposure: Without a program the practice cannot show that an error was an honest mistake caught by its own controls. That record is one of the things that can make the difference between a refund and penalties.
recommended_review: With the attorney, write a short program sized to two clinicians. Start with the audit, because its results decide everything else.
control: A named compliance contact who, where possible, is not the owner and does not prepare claims (a staff member or an outside consultant), reporting to the owner each quarter. An annual training hour, a quarterly chart audit, a log of issues and corrections, and a yearly review by the auditor of the billing rules for visits and write-offs.

title: Possible overpayments with a legal deadline once identified
what_we_see: Two patterns in this review could each mean Medicare paid more than the records support: visit levels and advance care planning. Two others raise different questions. If long-term residents were billed as skilled stays, Medicare paid less in 2026, not more. The initial visits billed under the nurse practitioner's code raise a facility rule; Medicare allowed them at her 85% rate, and past claims are not being reopened. A third pattern that could mean Medicare pays more than it owes was found on November 10, 2026: 148 October visits went in under the physician although the feed names the nurse practitioner on them. 120 of their lines are at Medicare and none was paid by November 10. If Medicare pays them under the physician, about 15% of each payment is more than it owes on every visit that was the nurse practitioner's. None has been tested against charts.
rule: A provider must report and return an overpayment within 60 days of identifying it. Since January 1, 2025 an overpayment is identified when the provider knows of it, deliberately avoids learning of it, or recklessly disregards the information in hand. That is the False Claims Act meaning of "knowingly". Once a first overpayment is identified, a timely, good-faith investigation of related overpayments suspends the deadline until the total is calculated or 180 days after that first identification, whichever comes first. The lookback is six years.
exposure: Money kept after the deadline can become a false claim: three times the amount plus a penalty of $14,308 to $28,619 for each claim at current levels. Acting promptly and on advice keeps a billing problem a refund.
recommended_review: Have the attorney open and direct the review of visit levels, and set the sample plan with the auditor. Give the attorney the history first: why top-level hospital visits fell to 1.3% in 2024 and rose again, and any audit, record request, denial pattern or advice from that time. Earlier notice changes the legal position. Record the date the review starts and the date each overpayment is identified. The 60 days run from identification. A prompt, good-faith review of related claims pauses them from the day it starts, for no more than 180 days after the first identification.
control: A standing rule: any audit finding of an overpayment goes to the attorney the same week, with a dated record of what was decided. The attorney chooses the route: a voluntary refund to the Medicare contractor for an ordinary error, the Inspector General's self-disclosure protocol where penalties could apply (at least 1.5 times what Medicare paid, and never less than $20,000), or the Medicare agency's protocol for a problem under the self-referral law alone. The deadline to return the money is suspended once a protocol filing is acknowledged or an extended repayment schedule is requested.

title: Medical director payments that may come from facilities where the practice also treats residents
what_we_see: The practice received two medical director stipends in the first nine months of 2026, $12,000 each. The data in hand do not name the payers. If they are facilities whose residents the practice also treats and bills for, the payments must fit the rule below. Whether written agreements, fair-market-value support and time records exist has not been confirmed.
rule: A physician who is paid by a facility and also sends it business (admissions, therapy orders, certifications of skilled care) has a financial relationship that must fit an exception to the federal self-referral law and should fit an Anti-Kickback safe harbor: a signed written agreement of at least a year, pay set in advance at fair market value, not tied to the volume or value of referrals, and for services actually performed and documented. Florida's kickback and patient-brokering laws cover referrals in either direction, for every payer.
exposure: If an agreement fails the exception, the facility may not bill Medicare for the designated services the physician ordered there, such as therapy billed to Part B, and must repay what it collected. The physician can face a civil penalty for each such service he knew or should have known was barred. Under the Anti-Kickback Statute, a claim that results from a kickback counts as a false claim, and penalties and exclusion can follow. Regulators have specifically warned about medical director agreements with little documented work.
recommended_review: Collect every medical director agreement from the past six years, not only the two current ones, with the fair-market-value support and time records for each. Stipends were $185,300 in 2023. Have the attorney confirm each fits the personal services exception and safe harbor. If a directorship is at a nursing home, check it against Florida's rule: medical director certification held or in progress, a documented facility visit every month, and a quarterly meeting with the facility's risk and quality committee.
control: A monthly time log for each directorship, signed by the physician and sent to the facility, and a calendar reminder 90 days before each agreement ends.

title: Enrollment and credentialing gaps; the physician's Medicaid agreement expires December 27
what_we_see: Several enrollment problems are open. The physician's Florida Medicaid provider agreement expires December 27, 2026; the renewal is to be filed by November 13 (December 1 is the last call), and nothing shows it has been filed. The nurse practitioner's Florida Medicaid enrollment is a new application, not a renewal: her old Medicaid number ended, and the agency returned the application with three faults. A commercial plan terminated the practice after a missed recredentialing. TRICARE For Life's electronic enrollment was rejected. The nurse practitioner's national provider record is out of date. Three items in the earlier plan were out of date and are corrected (November 10, 2026): the UnitedHealthcare directory attestation is not overdue (done August 28, next about November 26), TRICARE East's electronic claims were approved in October, and Railroad Medicare is paying ($718.76 in 2026, $3,764 open).
rule: A claim is payable only if the clinician was enrolled with that payer on the date of service. Florida Medicaid enrollment is what lets the practice be paid by Medicaid and by Medicaid managed care plans, and order or refer services for Medicaid patients. It adds little secondary payment on dual-eligible patients, who are about four in ten of the practice's Medicare patients: Florida pays nothing toward Medicare coinsurance when Medicare has already paid at least the Medicaid rate.
exposure: Denied Medicaid and Medicaid-plan claims until fixed, a plan's duty to drop a provider who is not enrolled with the State, denied claims for services the physician orders for Medicaid patients, and services that can never be billed for the gap period. 108 denied visits are already tagged credentialing.
recommended_review: Reset the Florida Medicaid portal password (it expired November 4 unless it was changed), file the renewal in that portal by November 13 (December 1 is the last call) and get written confirmation. Then rank the remaining items by dollars affected.
control: One calendar of every enrollment, license and registration expiry for both clinicians with 90-day warnings, checked at the monthly review. The practice's sheet 'Practice compliance & renewals calendar' mirrors to Google Calendar; 22 rows were added on November 10, 2026.

title: The practice depends on one physician and a few sites
what_we_see: The owner bills 76.8% of charges, holds the facility and hospital relationships, manages the finances and maintains the billing rulebook. One hospital is 37.8% of charges and the top three sites are 64.8%. Medical director stipends have fallen from $185,300 in 2023 to about $32,000 a year.
rule: This is a business risk, not a rule. Insurers, lenders and buyers all ask the same question: what happens to revenue if the owner is out, or if the largest site changes its physician coverage.
exposure: An illness, a change of hospital administration or the loss of one facility could remove a third or more of revenue within weeks. The same dependence is the main reason a buyer would discount the price.
recommended_review: Write down what would happen in each case and what it would cost.
control: A covering physician under written agreement, a second clinician known at every site, disability and key-person insurance, and written agreements with the main facilities.

title: Software agents act on billing rules that have not been independently reviewed
what_we_see: Agents enter charges, send claims, post payments, re-send denied claims and write off old balances every few hours under a written rulebook. Rules include writing off balances over a year old ($40,686 on November 2, 2026) and re-dating a care-management claim to month end after a frequency denial. This application also allows anyone to create a sign-in. Since a check added on November 10, 2026, only an approved address that has been confirmed can see data. On November 10, 2026 an independent review of a new place-of-service rule found an older defect in the charge import: it had entered 149 October visits under the other clinician (see that finding). The same day two read-only reviews proved that the insurance check had logged success on 84 feed visits that could never bill (see that finding). The check had also added 56 plans found only by discovery, in 13 batches, without a person; one was a dental plan added by mistake. The owner said on November 10 that such plans may keep being added, only medical plans active on the date of service; that check came with rule version .7, which went live at 01:20 UTC on November 11, 2026 after three independent reviews, a fix round and a re-check. The first version of the place-of-service rule went to the live billing branch on the owner's word before its review had finished. The reviewed version 2026-11-10.4 replaced it at 11:14 UTC, after a confirming review of that exact version came back clean, and version .6 went live at 22:46 UTC after three independent reviews, a fix round and a re-check.
rule: The practice is responsible for every claim submitted in its name, whoever or whatever prepares it. Under the False Claims Act, knowing includes reckless disregard, with no proof of intent needed. Florida's Medicaid law gives the provider an affirmative duty to supervise the preparation and submission of claims. Changing a code, date, modifier or diagnosis after a denial is acceptable only when the record supports the change and a qualified person has checked it. A Medicare denial is a payment decision. It stands unless it is reopened or appealed. A claim is sent again only when it was rejected as incomplete or when First Coast's instructions for that denial say to resubmit. Re-sending paid or denied claims produces duplicate denials, and the share of claims denied is one of the things Medicare weighs when it decides whether to revoke billing privileges. Routinely waiving Medicare copayments and deductibles is unlawful. A patient's balance may be written off for documented hardship or after a real effort to collect has failed. The opposite rule applies to Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, a group that includes most dual-eligible patients nationally: federal law forbids billing them for Medicare cost sharing at all. Every write-off therefore needs a reason code.
exposure: An automated rule that is wrong is wrong on every claim it touches, and it leaves a complete log of having done so. In 2025 a physician group paid $45 million over allegations that its billing software was set to bill the higher-paid service every time.
recommended_review: Have the coding auditor read every rule that changes a code, date, modifier, diagnosis, place of service or balance, and sample 25 automated actions against the charts. The rules for care-management claims, and the actions taken under them, are left out of that reading and that sample. The owner confirmed on November 10, 2026 that consent, care plans and time records are on file for these claims. Confirm that the automatic write-off rule touches insurance balances only and records a reason. List every rule that re-sends a claim Medicare has already paid or denied. Check each against First Coast's instructions: reopening, appeal or, where allowed, a corrected new claim.
control: The owner's written approval for any rule that changes a claim's code, date, modifier, diagnosis, place of service or balance. A monthly sample of automated actions. Open sign-up turned off and access keys rotated. A rule that changes what goes on a claim goes live only after an independent review of that exact version is back, unless the owner says in writing to deliver first. A routine reads back what it saved before it logs success.

title: Medicare quality program: a 9% cut is set for the nurse practitioner in 2027, and about 9% is expected for both clinicians in 2028 unless 2026 is reported
what_we_see: Both clinicians must take part. For 2022 to 2024 CMS excused them automatically after declared disasters, with a neutral score of 75. For 2025 nothing was reported. CMS scored the physician on the hospital's results, because 95% of his Medicare services in the measuring period were in the hospital: 65.81 points and a 1.10% cut. It scored the nurse practitioner on cost alone: 16.31 points and the full 9% cut. Both cuts apply to Medicare Part B payments from January 1, 2027. For 2026 the physician no longer meets the hospital test (64% of his Medicare lines in the measuring period, 42% in the latest year), so with nothing reported both clinicians are scored on cost alone. On November 10, 2026 the owner told billing to add the advance care plan code to the next Medicare claim of every patient 65 or older, once per patient, and registered the group and both clinicians for the reporting option Quality Care for Patients with Neurological Conditions (M0004). The code, 1123F, says that an advance care plan or a named decision-maker is documented in the patient's record. Asked on November 10, 2026 whether this holds for every patient the practice follows, the owner answered 'yes for all', so the statement on each claim is his, and CMS can ask for the record of any coded patient. A patient who declined needs code 1124F, which is not in AdvancedMD's code list, and one with whom it was never discussed needs 1123F with modifier 8P. A person enters both, and the owner names those patients. The first registration that day was for Value in Primary Care; it was changed after an independent check of the 2026 options showed that the neurological option, whose only claims measure is the advance care plan, scores better for the same code. M0004 is in AdvancedMD's code list. Rule version 2026-11-10.6, live on the billing branch since 22:46 UTC on November 10, adds the no-charge code 1123F from the next feed import: up to three lines first, on Medicare patients 65 and older and never on hospital visits; once one is seen billed, more visits carry it and M0004 goes once on one claim for each clinician. The rule adds the code only to visits dated in 2026: from January 1, 2027 it adds none until the owner renews it. On the owner's word ('doesnt appear to have any significance whiever way to just deal with it'), a visit held only because of its no-charge line has that line taken off and goes out.
rule: Below 75 points the cut is 9% times the shortfall divided by 75, and a flat 9% at 18.75 points or fewer. A small practice needs one improvement activity for full credit in that category, 30 points of the 100. It is attested between January 4 and March 31, 2027 (8 p.m. Eastern) for the 2026 year, and the activity must have run 90 days in a row during 2026, so it must have been running by October 3, 2026. Quality codes go on Medicare claims with 2026 dates of service through December 31, 2026, and those claims must be processed by March 1, 2027. For the 2026 score the number of coded lines does not matter: at least one counted line and M0004 once for each clinician are what count. Both clinicians had a 10-point bonus for complex patients in 2025; it counts only when something is submitted, and the 2026 amount is not known. A small practice that reports through a reporting option needs only that option's claim measures: Value in Primary Care has four, the neurological option has one, the advance care plan. A registration can be changed until November 30, 2026, 8 p.m. Eastern. The exception application is for rare events outside the practice's control and closes December 31, 2026.
exposure: 2027: about $16,500 to $18,000, already set by the 2025 scores (about $4,800 to $5,700 for the physician and $11,700 to $12,200 for the nurse practitioner). 2028: about 9% for both if nothing is reported for 2026. This is an estimate: it is 9% if each cost score is 62.5 or lower, as the nurse practitioner's was in 2025, and about 6.3% at a median cost score. Medicare Part B for the two clinicians is projected at $567,280 for 2026 (range $522,000 to $597,000; the method missed by up to 9% on earlier years), so 9% is about $47,000 to $54,000. Attesting one improvement activity alone brings the estimated score to about 56 and the cut to about 2.2%, about $12,000 to $13,600. Under the neurological option, with the advance care plan code on 2026 claims, M0004 on one claim for each clinician and one activity attested, the estimate is at least 69 points, and 95 if cost is not scored; 75 or more means no cut. The same code on the ordinary route gives at most 66. These are estimates: the 56 assumes a cost score like the nurse practitioner's 2025 score of 54 and the same 10-point bonus. The Medicare amounts are AdvancedMD's posted payments.
recommended_review: Done on November 10, 2026: status looked up; the 2025 feedback and payment adjustment read; the group and both clinicians registered for the neurological option (M0004); M0004 found in AdvancedMD's code list; the quality code live in billing (version .6); 34 calendar entries, 22 rows in the compliance sheet and 3 new rows on the Credentialing Board, with the attestation set for Monday January 4, 2027 at 9:00 AM. Next: the owner names the one improvement activity both clinicians carried out 90 days in a row in 2026, and its proof file is built. Then six entries at qpp.cms.gov between January 4 and March 31, 2027: the group and each clinician, under the option and under traditional reporting.
control: A calendar, now set up. November 30, 2026, 8 p.m. Eastern: last day to change the registration. December 31, 2026: last date of service for 2026 claim codes and last day for an exception application. March 1, 2027: claims with quality codes must be processed. January 4 to March 31, 2027: the attestation. The CMS sign-in password must be changed every 60 days. For 2027 the owner renews the quality-code rule before January 1; then the codes go on every eligible Medicare claim and are checked monthly. One improvement activity is named in January, with its proof filed as the year goes.

title: Thin cash and expensive debt against an audit or a lost site
what_we_see: Cash covers about 48 days of spending. The main loan costs 13.99%. The owner drew $311,241 in salary and distributions in nine months and owes the corporation $162,121.
rule: Not a rule. Medicare can suspend payments or require repayment during an audit, and it is 55.5% of charges.
exposure: A payment hold or a refund demand of even $100,000 would exceed the cash on hand.
recommended_review: With the accountant, set a cash floor and a plan for the loan and the amount owed by the owner.
control: A 13-week cash forecast, a 90-day cash floor before distributions, and an unused line of credit.

title: Advance care planning billed without a tested record of time and consent
what_we_see: Advance care planning (99497) was billed on 62 encounters in the charge feed, about 8% of face-to-face visits, usually on the same day as an admission or another visit. In CMS data the two clinicians billed it about 650 to 880 times a year from 2019 to 2024. In the 2024 public data the nurse practitioner billed it 610 times against about 1,950 visits, including 168 times against 210 home or assisted living visits, and the two clinicians billed 878 claims for at most 614 patients. Whether each note records the time and who took part has not been checked.
rule: The conversation must be voluntary, and the note should say so, explain advance directives, name who was present, and state the minutes. The first code needs at least 16 minutes. Billing it again for the same patient needs a documented change in health or wishes. Time counted here cannot also count toward the visit billed the same day. From January 1, 2027, planning done by staff uses separate codes.
exposure: Nationally 29.8% of the dollars paid for this code were improper in Medicare's 2025 review, nine in ten for insufficient documentation. A claim with no time recorded can be denied in full. At 650 to 880 claims a year, Medicare allowed about $55,000 a year for these, and about $220,000 in the public data for 2021 through 2024. It is an easy finding for a reviewer.
recommended_review: Include 10 advance care planning notes in the outside audit.
control: A note template that will not release the code without minutes, participants and a statement that the discussion was voluntary.

title: Complex chronic care management: records confirmed by the owner
what_we_see: In October 2026 the practice billed the complex care-management code (99487) for 257 patients, 213 of them with the add-on code (99489), all under the physician. The owner confirmed on November 10, 2026 that consent, care plans and time records are on file for these claims. No review is planned. The open question on this line is collection: only about 42% of these lines have been paid since June. Of October's lines, 152 carry place of service 31 (skilled stay) and 103 carry place of service 13 (assisted living). Since November 10, 2026 the charge import enters care management in the five nursing buildings as place of service 32, except in a month the chart looks skilled (see the place-of-service finding).
rule: Each claim rests on: two or more chronic conditions expected to last at least 12 months; the patient's consent before care management starts; a comprehensive care plan; at least 60 minutes that month of care-management time by clinical staff under the billing practitioner's direction, toward which the practitioner's own time also counts (30 more for each add-on); and medical decisions of moderate or high complexity. Medicare's guidance allows the service for residents of nursing and assisted living facilities and says to report the place of service where the practitioner would ordinarily see the patient.
exposure: None is flagged. This is a revenue line of about $165,000 a year at October's volume and today's paid rate, and about $370,000 a year if every line were paid.
recommended_review: None planned, at the owner's direction.
control: Keep each month's consent, care plan and time log where they can be pulled by patient and month. Place of service is set by the import's rule (32 in a nursing building, 31 in a month the chart looks skilled), backed by each facility's Part A list. Never use a date of service after the patient's date of death, and do not bill care management in a month when hospice or home health supervision (G0182 or G0181) is billed.
